analysis.one_liner: Lets regulators force natural gas pipeline companies to refund excessive charges to customers with interest.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal natural gas law so that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which regulates interstate natural gas pipelines, can order gas companies to refund customers—with interest—for rates or charges found to be unjust or unreasonable. It would also shift the burden of proof onto the gas company to justify a rate change, require refunds to cover a window of up to 150 days after a complaint is filed, and require FERC to decide these cases within 180 days or explain why it hasn't.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that buy natural gas delivered through interstate pipelines. When FERC later finds a pipeline charged more than a just and reasonable rate, customers would get money back with interest, instead of the company simply keeping the difference while the case is decided.

how_it_helps.text: FERC would be required to order natural gas companies to refund, with interest, amounts charged above the just and reasonable rate, paid to the people who actually paid those charges.

At any hearing over a rate change, the burden of proof would fall on the natural gas company to show the new rate is just and reasonable, rather than on regulators or consumers to prove it is excessive.
Refunds would reach back to a set 'refund effective date'—up to 150 days after a complaint is filed—so companies could not run out the clock while a case is pending.
FERC would have to decide these rate cases within 180 days or publicly explain the delay and estimate when it will decide, and could require a company to post a bond while a rate change is pending.

analysis.who_pays: Interstate natural gas pipeline companies, which would face mandatory refunds with interest, a bond requirement, the burden of proving their own rates are justified, and tighter deadlines on rate cases. Those costs could in some cases flow into the rates companies seek in future proceedings.

drawbacks.text: The bill itself directs FERC to study, three to four years after enactment, whether the new refund rules raise the cost of capital for natural gas companies—acknowledging the concern that higher financial risk for pipeline companies could eventually show up in the rates customers pay.
The rules would apply only to proceedings started after enactment, so past overcharges in already-pending cases would not be refundable, though those cases could be withdrawn and refiled.

A good-faith objection is that shifting the burden of proof and mandating fast refunds could make pipeline financing more expensive or discourage investment in gas infrastructure; supporters of the current system argue existing FERC processes already balance these concerns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and concrete: customers recover money when regulators find a pipeline overcharged them, and the company—not the consumer—has to prove a rate hike is fair. The main cost is potentially higher financing costs for pipeline companies, which could eventually touch customer rates; the bill acknowledges this by requiring a study of that exact question. On balance it is a consumer-protection measure with a real, if modest, downside risk that the bill itself flags for study.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on April 18, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action was taken: the bill never received a committee hearing or markup, never reached the Senate floor, and received no House action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill drew one cosponsor, a Republican, giving it bipartisan sponsorship but very little visible support in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Interstate natural gas pipeline companies are better off: they continue operating under existing rules under which customers can be charged contested rates for long stretches with no automatic refund, and no burden of proof on the company. Customers who paid potentially excessive rates received nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, so it had bipartisan sponsorship, but with no votes ever taken there is no record of how the parties would have lined up.

industries.note: The bill would require them to refund excessive rates with interest, post bonds during rate disputes, and prove their own rate changes are justified—costs that under current rules can stay with customers. Its interest in the bill ran directly against the customers it bills.
Distribution utilities and the households and businesses they serve would benefit when pipeline overcharges are refunded with interest, since regulated pipeline costs flow through into gas bills.
